claim: α-Synuclein (αSyn) promotes membrane fusion and fission by interacting with various negatively charged phospholipids.
source: The Parkinson's disease protein α-synuclein (αSyn) promotes membrane fusion and fission by interacting with various negatively charged phospholipids.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about αSyn function.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) mediate plasma membrane localization of endogenous αSyn in A2780, HeLa, SK-MEL-2, and differentiated and undifferentiated neuronal SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Here, we show that phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3), two highly acidic components of inner PM leaflets, mediate PM localization of endogenous pools of αSyn in A2780, HeLa, SK-MEL-2, and differentiated and undifferentiated neuronal SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental observations in multiple cell lines.

claim: αSyn binds to reconstituted PIP2 membranes in a helical conformation in vitro.
source: We demonstrate that αSyn binds to reconstituted PIP2 membranes in a helical conformation in vitro
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy and NMR experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: PIP2 synthesizing kinases and hydrolyzing phosphatases reversibly redistribute αSyn in cells.
source: We demonstrate that αSyn binds to reconstituted PIP2 membranes in a helical conformation in vitro and that PIP2 synthesizing kinases and hydrolyzing phosphatases reversibly redistribute αSyn in cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with PIPKIγ overexpression and phosphatase expression shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: αSyn-PM targeting follows phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3K)-dependent changes of cellular PIP2 and PIP3 levels.
source: We further delineate that αSyn-PM targeting follows phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3K)-dependent changes of cellular PIP2 and PIP3 levels
evidence: This is demonstrated through histamine and insulin stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Aggregates of human α-synuclein (αSyn) constitute the main components of Lewy body inclusions in Parkinson's disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies.
source: Aggregates of human α-synuclein (αSyn) constitute the main components of Lewy body inclusions in Parkinson's disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies (Goedert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goedert et al., 2013.

claim: αSyn is abundantly found in different types of neurons in the brain, where it primarily localizes to presynaptic terminals.
source: In the brain, αSyn is abundantly found in different types of neurons, where it primarily localizes to presynaptic terminals and regulates synaptic vesicle (SV) clustering and trafficking (Sulzer and Edwards, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sulzer and Edwards, 2019.

claim: αSyn regulates synaptic vesicle (SV) clustering and trafficking.
source: In the brain, αSyn is abundantly found in different types of neurons, where it primarily localizes to presynaptic terminals and regulates synaptic vesicle (SV) clustering and trafficking (Sulzer and Edwards, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sulzer and Edwards, 2019.

claim: Isolated αSyn is disordered in solution.
source: Isolated αSyn is disordered in solution, whereas residues 1–100 adopt extended or kinked helical conformations upon binding to membranes containing negatively charged phospholipids (Fusco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fusco et al., 2018.

claim: Residues 1–100 of αSyn adopt extended or kinked helical conformations upon binding to membranes containing negatively charged phospholipids.
source: Isolated αSyn is disordered in solution, whereas residues 1–100 adopt extended or kinked helical conformations upon binding to membranes containing negatively charged phospholipids (Fusco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fusco et al., 2018.

claim: Complementary electrostatic contacts between lysine residues within αSyn's N-terminal KTKEGV-repeats and acidic phospholipid headgroups align α-helices on membrane surfaces.
source: Complementary electrostatic contacts between lysine residues within αSyn's N-terminal KTKEGV-repeats and acidic phospholipid headgroups align these α-helices on respective membrane surfaces (Snead and Eliezer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Snead and Eliezer, 2019.

claim: Membrane curvature acts as a determinant for αSyn membrane binding.
source: Membrane curvature (Middleton and Rhoades, 2010), lipid packing defects (Nuscher et al., 2004; Pranke et al., 2011) and fatty acid compositions (Fortin et al., 2004; Galvagnion, 2017) act as additional determinants for membrane binding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Middleton and Rhoades, 2010.

claim: Lipid packing defects act as determinants for αSyn membrane binding.
source: Membrane curvature (Middleton and Rhoades, 2010), lipid packing defects (Nuscher et al., 2004; Pranke et al., 2011) and fatty acid compositions (Fortin et al., 2004; Galvagnion, 2017) act as additional determinants for membrane binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nuscher et al., 2004 and Pranke et al., 2011.

claim: Fatty acid compositions act as determinants for αSyn membrane binding.
source: Membrane curvature (Middleton and Rhoades, 2010), lipid packing defects (Nuscher et al., 2004; Pranke et al., 2011) and fatty acid compositions (Fortin et al., 2004; Galvagnion, 2017) act as additional determinants for membrane binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fortin et al., 2004 and Galvagnion, 2017.

claim: αSyn remodels target membranes.
source: αSyn remodels target membranes (Varkey et al., 2010; Westphal and Chandra, 2013), which likely relates to its biological function(s) in vesicle docking, fusion and fission (Sulzer and Edwards, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Varkey et al., 2010 and Westphal and Chandra, 2013.

claim: αSyn membrane remodeling likely relates to its biological function(s) in vesicle docking, fusion and fission.
source: αSyn remodels target membranes (Varkey et al., 2010; Westphal and Chandra, 2013), which likely relates to its biological function(s) in vesicle docking, fusion and fission (Sulzer and Edwards, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from membrane remodeling observations and cited literature.

claim: αSyn multimerization and aggregation may initiate at membrane surfaces.
source: Furthermore, αSyn multimerization and aggregation may initiate at membrane surfaces, which holds important ramifications for possible cellular scenarios in PD (Galvagnion, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Galvagnion, 2017.

claim: Early αSyn oligomers bind to and disrupt cellular and reconstituted membranes.
source: Early αSyn oligomers bind to and disrupt cellular and reconstituted membranes (Reynolds et al., 2011; Fusco et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reynolds et al., 2011 and Fusco et al., 2017.

claim: Mature αSyn aggregates are found closely associated with membranous cell structures and intact organelles in cellular models of Lewy body inclusions.
source: whereas mature aggregates are found closely associated with membranous cell structures and intact organelles in cellular models of Lewy body inclusions (Mahul-Mellier et al., 2020) and in postmortem brain sections of PD patients (Shahmoradian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mahul-Mellier et al., 2020.

claim: Mature αSyn aggregates are found closely associated with membranous cell structures and intact organelles in postmortem brain sections of PD patients.
source: whereas mature aggregates are found closely associated with membranous cell structures and intact organelles in cellular models of Lewy body inclusions (Mahul-Mellier et al., 2020) and in postmortem brain sections of PD patients (Shahmoradian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shahmoradian et al., 2019.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol phosphates (PIPs) are integral components of cell membranes and a universal class of acidic phospholipids with key functions in biology.
source: Phosphatidylinositol phosphates (PIPs) are integral components of cell membranes and a universal class of acidic phospholipids with key functions in biology (Balla, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balla, 2013.

claim: Reversible phosphorylation of PIP inositol headgroups at positions 3, 4 and 5 generates seven types of PIPs.
source: Reversible phosphorylation of their inositol headgroups at positions 3, 4 and 5 generates seven types of PIPs, which act as selective binding sites for folded and disordered PIP-interaction domains (Balla, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balla, 2005.

claim: PIPs act as selective binding sites for folded and disordered PIP-interaction domains.
source: Reversible phosphorylation of their inositol headgroups at positions 3, 4 and 5 generates seven types of PIPs, which act as selective binding sites for folded and disordered PIP-interaction domains (Balla, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balla, 2005.

claim: PIPs make up less than 2% of total phospholipids in eukaryotic cells.
source: In eukaryotic cells, PIPs make up less than 2% of total phospholipids with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, PI(4,5)P2 or PIP2 hereafter, as the most common species (McLaughlin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLaughlin et al., 2002.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is the most common PIP species in eukaryotic cells.
source: In eukaryotic cells, PIPs make up less than 2% of total phospholipids with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, PI(4,5)P2 or PIP2 hereafter, as the most common species (McLaughlin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLaughlin et al., 2002.

claim: PIPs function as core determinants of organelle identity.
source: PIPs function as core determinants of organelle identity (Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Di Paolo and De Camilli, 2006.

claim: PIP2 is predominantly found at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: PIP2 is predominantly found at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM), where it acts as a signaling scaffold and protein-recruitment platform (McLaughlin and Murray, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLaughlin and Murray, 2005.

claim: PIP2 acts as a signaling scaffold and protein-recruitment platform at the plasma membrane.
source: PIP2 is predominantly found at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM), where it acts as a signaling scaffold and protein-recruitment platform (McLaughlin and Murray, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLaughlin and Murray, 2005.

claim: PIP2 carries a negative net charge of −4 at pH 7.
source: Carrying a negative net charge of −4 at pH 7 renders it more acidic than other cellular phospholipids such as phosphatidylserine (net charge −1) or phosphatidic acid (net charge −1) (Kooijman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooijman et al., 2009.

claim: PIP2 is more acidic than phosphatidylserine and phosphatidic acid.
source: Carrying a negative net charge of −4 at pH 7 renders it more acidic than other cellular phospholipids such as phosphatidylserine (net charge −1) or phosphatidic acid (net charge −1) (Kooijman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooijman et al., 2009.

claim: Disordered PIP2-binding domains contain stretches of polybasic residues that establish complementary electrostatic contacts with negatively charged PIP head groups.
source: Disordered PIP2-binding domains contain stretches of polybasic residues that establish complementary electrostatic contacts with the negatively charged PIP head groups (McLaughlin et al., 2002) reminiscent of how αSyn KTKEGV-lysines interact with acidic phospholipids (Dettmer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McLaughlin et al., 2002 and Dettmer, 2018.

claim: αSyn has been shown to bind to reconstituted PIP2 vesicles in vitro.
source: Indeed, αSyn has been shown to bind to reconstituted PIP2 vesicles in vitro (Narayanan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Narayanan et al., 2005.

claim: PIP3 harbors an additional phosphate group compared to PIP2, which renders it more acidic with a net charge of −5 at pH 7.
source: Phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate, PI(3,4,5)P3 or PIP3 hereafter, harbors an additional phosphate group, which renders it even more acidic (net charge −5 at pH 7) (Kooijman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooijman et al., 2009.

claim: The steady-state abundance of PIP3 at the plasma membrane is low.
source: The steady-state abundance of PIP3 at the PM is low (Balla, 2013), but local levels increase dynamically in response to cell signaling, especially following phosphatidylinositide-3 kinase (PI3K) activation (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balla, 2013.

claim: Local PIP3 levels increase dynamically in response to cell signaling, especially following PI3K activation.
source: The steady-state abundance of PIP3 at the PM is low (Balla, 2013), but local levels increase dynamically in response to cell signaling, especially following phosphatidylinositide-3 kinase (PI3K) activation (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bilanges et al., 2019.

claim: Endogenous αSyn forms discrete foci at the plasma membrane of human A2780, HeLa, SK-MEL-2 and neuronal SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Using confocal and total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, we show that endogenous αSyn forms discrete foci at the PM of human A2780, HeLa, SK-MEL-2 and neuronal SH-SY5Y cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The abundance and localization of endogenous αSyn foci at the plasma membrane correlate with pools of PM PIP2 and PIP3.
source: The abundance and localization of these foci correlate with pools of PM PIP2 and PIP3.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through colocalization experiments shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: αSyn binds PIP2 membranes in its characteristic, helical conformation.
source: We further delineate high-resolution insights into αSyn interactions with reconstituted PIP2 vesicles by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and establish that αSyn binds PIP2 membranes in its characteristic, helical conformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR and CD spectroscopy experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Confocal immunofluorescence localization in A2780 cells revealed a speckled intracellular distribution of αSyn with distinct foci at apical and basal PM regions.
source: Confocal immunofluorescence (IF) localization in A2780 cells with an antibody that specifically recognizes αSyn without cross-reacting with its β and γ isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) revealed a speckled intracellular distribution with distinct αSyn foci at apical and basal PM regions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1A and antibody specificity shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: siRNA-mediated gene silencing of αSyn established that αSyn foci corresponded to endogenous protein pools.
source: We verified overall antibody specificity by downregulating αSyn expression via siRNA-mediated gene silencing, which established that αSyn foci corresponded to endogenous protein pools (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In 10–20% of cases, clear superpositions of αSyn and PIP2 signals were detected at the basal plasma membrane of A2780 cells.
source: In 10–20% of cases, we detected clear superpositions of αSyn and PIP2 signals, which we confirmed by measuring fluorescence intensity profiles over individual cell cross-sections (Figure 1D, top panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through colocalization experiments shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Prominent pools of αSyn were found in expanded structures reminiscent of synaptic boutons along neurites in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells, where they colocalized with PIP2.
source: We found prominent pools of αSyn in expanded structures reminiscent of synaptic boutons along neurites, where they colocalized with PIP2 (Figure 1C, bottom panel, Figure 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy of differentiated SH-SY5Y cells shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Structures containing αSyn and PIP2 in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells also stained positive for the presynaptic V-SNARE component synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2.
source: These structures also stained positive for the presynaptic V-SNARE component syanptobrevin-2/VAMP2, a known binding partner of αSyn (Burré et al., 2010; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through colocalization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and supported by citation to Burré et al., 2010.

claim: Transient overexpression of GFP-tagged PIPKIγ increased amounts of αSyn at the plasma membrane of transfected cells.
source: Upon kinase expression, confirmed by GFP fluorescence, we detected increased amounts of αSyn at the PM of transfected cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PIPKIγ overexpression experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression of GFP alone did not alter PM levels of αSyn.
source: By contrast, expression of GFP alone did not alter PM levels of αSyn.
evidence: This is demonstrated through control experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Transient PIPKIγ expression did not affect overall αSyn abundance.
source: We obtained similar results in undifferentiated SH-SY5Y and HeLa cells (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1) and confirmed that transient PIPKIγ expression did not affect overall αSyn abundance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blot experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Endogenous αSyn was detected at PM foci in A2780, HeLa, SH-SY5Y and SK-MEL-2 cells by TIRF microscopy.
source: Employing a narrow evanescent field depth of ~50 nm, we detected endogenous αSyn at PM foci in A2780, HeLa, SH-SY5Y and SK-MEL-2 cells, which correlated with total αSyn levels determined by semi-quantitative western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through TIRF microscopy and western blotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: N-terminally acetylated αSyn added to reconstituted PIP2 vesicles showed characteristic helical signatures by circular dichroism spectroscopy.
source: Circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy revealed characteristic helical signatures (Davidson et al., 1998; Jo et al., 2000; Figure 2A)
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy experiments shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: NMR experiments confirmed site-selective line broadening of N-terminal residues 1–100 of αSyn upon binding to PIP2 vesicles, confirming membrane binding.
source: whereas NMR experiments confirmed site-selective line broadening of N-terminal residues 1–100, confirming membrane binding (Bodner et al., 2009; Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and supported by citations.

claim: Remodeled PIP2 vesicles with tubular extrusions were detected by negative-stain transmission electron microscopy after αSyn binding.
source: In line with these observations, we detected remodeled PIP2 vesicles by negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (EM), manifested by tubular extrusions emanating from reconstituted specimens and agreeing with published findings on other membrane systems (Varkey et al., 2010; Westphal and Chandra, 2013; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: Residues 1–100 of αSyn interacted with PIP2 vesicles in helical conformations that imposed membrane remodeling.
source: Together, these results established that residues 1–100 of αSyn interacted with PIP2 vesicles in helical conformations that imposed membrane remodeling, whereas its 40 C-terminal residues did not engage in membrane binding and remained flexible and disordered.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined CD, NMR, and EM data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 40 C-terminal residues of αSyn did not engage in membrane binding and remained flexible and disordered.
source: Together, these results established that residues 1–100 of αSyn interacted with PIP2 vesicles in helical conformations that imposed membrane remodeling, whereas its 40 C-terminal residues did not engage in membrane binding and remained flexible and disordered.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data showing observable C-terminal signals in Figure 2B.

claim: Up to a ~50-fold molar excess of lipid to protein, αSyn interacted with PC-PIP2 vesicles in a helical conformation without disrupting the monodisperse nature of the specimens.
source: Up to a ~50-fold molar excess of lipid to protein, αSyn interacted with PC-PIP2 vesicles in a helical conformation without disrupting the monodisperse nature of the specimens, that is, without membrane remodeling (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through CD spectroscopy and DLS experiments shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Residues 1–10 of αSyn constituted the primary interaction sites with PC-PIP2 vesicles.
source: Analyzing signal intensity ratios (I/I0) of unbound (I0) and PC-PIP2-bound αSyn (I), we found that residues 1–10 constituted the primary interaction sites, whereas residues 11–100 displayed progressively weaker membrane contacts.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR intensity ratio analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Residues 11–100 of αSyn displayed progressively weaker membrane contacts with PC-PIP2 vesicles compared to residues 1–10.
source: Analyzing signal intensity ratios (I/I0) of unbound (I0) and PC-PIP2-bound αSyn (I), we found that residues 1–10 constituted the primary interaction sites, whereas residues 11–100 displayed progressively weaker membrane contacts.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR intensity ratio analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C-terminal αSyn residues did not contribute to PC-PIP2 vesicle binding.
source: In agreement with our experiments on PIP2-only vesicles, we detected no contributions by C-terminal αSyn residues.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: N-terminally truncated αSyn lacking residues 1–4 (ΔN) did not bind to PC-PIP2 vesicles.
source: To further validate our conclusions, we performed NMR experiments with mutant forms of αSyn in which we deleted residues 1–4 (ΔN) (Bartels et al., 2010), substituted Phe4 and Tyr39 with alanine (F4A-Y39A) (Lokappa et al., 2014), or oxidized αSyn Met1, Met5, Met116 and Met123 to methionine-sulfoxides (MetOx) (Maltsev et al., 2013; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A). In line with earlier reports, we did not observe binding to PC-PIP2 vesicles for any of these variants.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with mutant αSyn shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and supported by citations.

claim: αSyn with Phe4 and Tyr39 substituted with alanine (F4A-Y39A) did not bind to PC-PIP2 vesicles.
source: To further validate our conclusions, we performed NMR experiments with mutant forms of αSyn in which we deleted residues 1–4 (ΔN) (Bartels et al., 2010), substituted Phe4 and Tyr39 with alanine (F4A-Y39A) (Lokappa et al., 2014), or oxidized αSyn Met1, Met5, Met116 and Met123 to methionine-sulfoxides (MetOx) (Maltsev et al., 2013; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A). In line with earlier reports, we did not observe binding to PC-PIP2 vesicles for any of these variants.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with mutant αSyn shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and supported by citations.

claim: Methionine-oxidized αSyn (MetOx) did not bind to PC-PIP2 vesicles.
source: To further validate our conclusions, we performed NMR experiments with mutant forms of αSyn in which we deleted residues 1–4 (ΔN) (Bartels et al., 2010), substituted Phe4 and Tyr39 with alanine (F4A-Y39A) (Lokappa et al., 2014), or oxidized αSyn Met1, Met5, Met116 and Met123 to methionine-sulfoxides (MetOx) (Maltsev et al., 2013; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A). In line with earlier reports, we did not observe binding to PC-PIP2 vesicles for any of these variants.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with mutant αSyn shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and supported by citations.

claim: PC-PIP2 interactions strongly depended on intact N-terminal αSyn residues, with critical contributions by Phe4 and Tyr39.
source: Our results corroborated that PC-PIP2 interactions strongly depended on intact N-terminal αSyn residues, with critical contributions by Phe4 and Tyr39, and requiring Met1 and Met5 in their reduced states.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PC-PIP2 interactions required Met1 and Met5 in their reduced states.
source: Our results corroborated that PC-PIP2 interactions strongly depended on intact N-terminal αSyn residues, with critical contributions by Phe4 and Tyr39, and requiring Met1 and Met5 in their reduced states.
evidence: This is inferred from the methionine oxidation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PLC addition to αSyn-bound PC-PIP2 vesicles led to recovery of αSyn NMR signals, indicating release of αSyn from membranes.
source: Indeed, we detected the recovery of αSyn NMR signals upon PLC addition (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with PLC shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Overall αSyn binding to PC-PIP2 vesicles was greatly reduced in the presence of calcium.
source: Whereas overall binding was greatly reduced, we found that the first 10 residues of αSyn displayed residual anchoring contacts with PC-PIP2 vesicles even at high (2.5 mM) calcium concentrations (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with calcium shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The first 10 residues of αSyn displayed residual anchoring contacts with PC-PIP2 vesicles even at high (2.5 mM) calcium concentrations.
source: Whereas overall binding was greatly reduced, we found that the first 10 residues of αSyn displayed residual anchoring contacts with PC-PIP2 vesicles even at high (2.5 mM) calcium concentrations (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 1), confirming earlier results on the stability of αSyn PC-PIP2 vesicle interactions in the presence of calcium (Narayanan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with calcium shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, and supported by citation.

claim: Hydrodynamic diameters of PC-PIP2 vesicles expanded upon PLC treatment.
source: Notably, DLS measurements showed that hydrodynamic diameters of PC-PIP2 vesicles expanded upon PLC treatment and in the presence of calcium, irrespective of whether αSyn was bound (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through DLS measurements shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Hydrodynamic diameters of PC-PIP2 vesicles expanded in the presence of calcium.
source: Notably, DLS measurements showed that hydrodynamic diameters of PC-PIP2 vesicles expanded upon PLC treatment and in the presence of calcium, irrespective of whether αSyn was bound (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through DLS measurements shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Vesicle remodeling and concomitant curvature reductions did not abolish αSyn interactions with PC-PIP2 vesicles.
source: This further suggested that vesicle remodeling and concomitant curvature reductions did not abolish αSyn interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the DLS and NMR data showing that αSyn remained bound despite vesicle expansion.

claim: αSyn did not bind to free inositol polyphosphate (IP6).
source: Surprisingly, we did not detect binding of αSyn to this highly negatively charged entity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), which insinuated that αSyn interactions with PIP-containing membranes required additional lipid contributions besides headgroup contacts.
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments with IP6 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: αSyn interactions with PIP-containing membranes required additional lipid contributions besides headgroup contacts.
source: Surprisingly, we did not detect binding of αSyn to this highly negatively charged entity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), which insinuated that αSyn interactions with PIP-containing membranes required additional lipid contributions besides headgroup contacts.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of binding to free IP6 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Only the conversion of PIP2 to PI(4)P by INPP5E led to a marked reduction of endogenous αSyn at the plasma membrane.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, only the conversion of PIP2 to PI(4)P by INPP5E led to a marked reduction of endogenous αSyn at the PM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phosphatase overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PM localization of cellular αSyn was modulated by PIP2-specific enzymes.
source: Together with earlier kinase results, these findings corroborated that PM localization of cellular αSyn was modulated by PIP2-specific enzymes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined kinase and phosphatase experiments shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: After 40 s of histamine stimulation, an initial increase of PIP2 and PIP3 levels at the PM was observed, which was mirrored by greater pools of endogenous αSyn at basal membrane regions.
source: After 40 s, we observed an initial increase of PIP2 and PIP3 levels at the PM, which was mirrored by greater pools of endogenous αSyn at basal membrane regions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PIP2 levels dropped at intermediate time points (85–120 s) after histamine stimulation, likely due to PLC-mediated PIP2 hydrolysis.
source: While PIP2 levels dropped at intermediate time points (85–120 s), likely due to PLC-mediated PIP2 hydrolysis, PIP3 concentrations were highest at 85 s and leveled off more slowly (120–240 s).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments shown in Figure 3B and inferred from known PLC activity.

claim: PIP3 concentrations were highest at 85 s after histamine stimulation and leveled off more slowly (120–240 s).
source: While PIP2 levels dropped at intermediate time points (85–120 s), likely due to PLC-mediated PIP2 hydrolysis, PIP3 concentrations were highest at 85 s and leveled off more slowly (120–240 s).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PM-αSyn followed the observed PIP3 behavior in a remarkably similar manner during histamine stimulation.
source: Interestingly, PM-αSyn followed the observed PIP3 behavior in a remarkably similar manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 240 s after histamine stimulation, a significant redistribution of cellular PIP2 and PIP3 pools toward the edges of SK-MEL-2 cells was noted, coinciding with the accumulation of bundled actin fibers.
source: At later time points (240 s), we noted a significant redistribution of cellular PIP2 and PIP3 pools toward the edges of SK-MEL-2 cells, coinciding with the accumulation of bundled actin fibers and in line with expected PI3K-signaling-dependent rearrangements of the cytoskeleton (Bilanges et al., 2019).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments shown in Figure 3B and supported by citation.

claim: αSyn colocalization with peripheral PIP2-PIP3 speckles at 240 s after histamine stimulation was significantly higher than at earlier time points.
source: αSyn colocalization with these peripheral PIP2-PIP3 speckles was significantly higher than at earlier time points (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-course experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Insulin stimulation of SK-MEL-2 cells for 10 min increased αSyn-PM localization.
source: In support of our hypothesis, we measured increased αSyn-PM localization by TIRF microscopy upon insulin stimulation for 10 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through insulin stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Observed PM accumulations of αSyn after histamine and insulin stimulation likely reflected enhanced recruitment of existing αSyn pools rather than de novo protein synthesis and PM targeting.
source: Given the short exposure times to histamine and insulin in these experiments, we reasoned that observed PM accumulations likely reflected enhanced recruitment of existing αSyn pools rather than de novo protein synthesis and PM targeting, thus providing further evidence that αSyn abundance at the PM correlated with signaling-dependent changes of PIP2 and PIP3 levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the short time scales of the stimulation experiments.

claim: Clusters of endogenous αSyn are found at the PM of human A2780, HeLa, SK-MEL-2 and SH-SY5Y cells, where their abundance correlates with PIP2 levels.
source: Our results establish that clusters of endogenous αSyn are found at the PM of human A2780, HeLa, SK-MEL-2 and SH-SY5Y cells, where their abundance correlates with PIP2 levels (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings demonstrated throughout the Results section.

claim: Targeted overexpression of the PIP2-generating kinase PIPKIγ increases αSyn at the PM.
source: Specifically, we show that targeted overexpression of the PIP2-generating kinase PIPKIγ increases αSyn at the PM (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is demonstrated through PIPKIγ overexpression experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The PIP2-specific phosphatase INPP5E reduces the amount of PM αSyn.
source: whereas the PIP2-specific phosphatase INPP5E reduces the amount of PM αSyn (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phosphatase overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PIP3-dependent histamine and insulin signaling redistributes αSyn to the PM.
source: We further demonstrate that PIP3-dependent histamine and insulin signaling redistributes αSyn to the PM (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated through histamine and insulin stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in PM PIP2 and PIP3 levels affect intracellular αSyn localization in a dynamic and reversible manner.
source: which collectively suggests that changes in PM PIP2 and PIP3 levels affect intracellular αSyn localization in a dynamic and reversible manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined kinase, phosphatase, and signaling experiments.

claim: αSyn directly interacts with reconstituted PIP2 vesicles in vitro.
source: While we cannot rule out that additional secondary protein–protein interactions contribute to PM targeting, we demonstrate that αSyn directly interacts with reconstituted PIP2 vesicles in vitro (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro binding experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The biophysical characteristics of αSyn-PIP2 interactions are indistinguishable from other previously identified, negatively charged membrane systems with primary contacts by N-terminal αSyn residues 1–10 and progressively weaker interactions along residues 11–100.
source: Importantly, the biophysical characteristics of these interactions are indistinguishable from other previously identified, negatively charged membrane systems with primary contacts by N-terminal αSyn residues 1–10 and progressively weaker interactions along residues 11–100.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the current NMR data with previously published results.

claim: The last 40, C-terminal residues of αSyn are not involved in PIP2 membrane binding, similar to all other reconstituted vesicular or planar lipid surface interactions studied thus far.
source: The last 40, C-terminal residues of αSyn are not involved in PIP2 membrane binding, similar to all other reconstituted vesicular or planar lipid surface interactions studied thus far (Bodner et al., 2009; Fusco et al., 2014; Perrin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated through NMR experiments and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIP2 and PIP3 constitute intuitive αSyn binding partners based on their highly acidic nature.
source: Based on the known preferences for negatively charged phospholipids, PIP2 and PIP3 constitute intuitive αSyn binding partners. Not only because of their highly acidic nature (Kooijman et al., 2009)
evidence: This is inferred from known properties of αSyn and PIPs, supported by citation.

claim: PIP2 and PIP3 acyl chain compositions contain saturated stearic-(18:0) and polyunsaturated arachidonic acids (20:4), conferring 'shallow' lipid packing defects that are ideally suited to accommodate αSyn's helical conformation(s).
source: but also because of their acyl chain compositions containing saturated stearic-(18:0) and polyunsaturated arachidonic acids (20:4), the latter conferring 'shallow' lipid packing defects (Bigay and Antonny, 2012) that are ideally suited to accommodate αSyn's helical conformation(s) (Pranke et al., 2011; Pinot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from known lipid properties and αSyn binding preferences, supported by citations.

claim: From a biophysical point of view, phosphatidylinositol polyphosphates satisfy many of the known requirements for efficient αSyn membrane binding.
source: Thus, from a biophysical point of view, phosphatidylinositol polyphosphates satisfy many of the known requirements for efficient αSyn membrane binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined biophysical properties discussed.

claim: PIPs are ubiquitously expressed and stringently required for exocytosis and endocytosis, especially in neurons.
source: From a biological point of view, PIPs are ubiquitously expressed and stringently required for exocytosis and endocytosis, especially in neurons, where highly abundant PIP2 and PIP3pools (up to ~6 mol%) mark SV uptake and release sites (James et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to James et al., 2008.

claim: Highly abundant PIP2 and PIP3 pools (up to ~6 mol%) mark synaptic vesicle uptake and release sites in neurons.
source: From a biological point of view, PIPs are ubiquitously expressed and stringently required for exocytosis and endocytosis, especially in neurons, where highly abundant PIP2 and PIP3pools (up to ~6 mol%) mark SV uptake and release sites (James et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to James et al., 2008.

claim: Multiple PIP-binding proteins mediate key steps in synaptic vesicle transmission and recycling.
source: Multiple PIP-binding proteins mediate key steps in SV transmission and recycling (Di Paolo et al., 2004; Milosevic et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Paolo et al., 2004 and Milosevic et al., 2005.

claim: αSyn has been implicated in synaptic exocytosis and endocytosis, but its role(s) in these processes is ill defined.
source: and, although, αSyn has been implicated in synaptic exocytosis and endocytosis, its role(s) in these processes is ill defined (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Endogenous levels of αSyn in the tested cell lines are low, particularly in comparison to presynaptic boutons, where αSyn concentrations reach up to 50 μM.
source: Endogenous levels of αSyn in the tested cell lines are low, particularly in comparison to presynaptic boutons, where αSyn concentrations reach up to 50 μM (Wilhelm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilhelm et al., 2014.

claim: The affinity of αSyn to PIP2 vesicles has been reported to be in the low μM range.
source: The affinity of αSyn to PIP2 vesicles has been reported to be in the low μM range (Narayanan and Scarlata, 2001), similar to most other reconstituted membrane systems containing negatively charged phospholipids (Middleton and Rhoades, 2010; Narayanan et al., 2005; Bodner et al., 2009; Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Fusco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Average dissociation constants for canonical PIP-binding scaffolds such as PH, C2, FYVE, and ENTH domains vary between μM and mM.
source: In comparison, average dissociation constants for canonical PIP-binding scaffolds such as PH, C2, FYVE, and ENTH domains vary between μM and mM (Balla, 2005; McLaughlin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Balla, 2005 and McLaughlin et al., 2002.

claim: Disordered polybasic PIP-binding motifs target negatively charged membranes with much weaker affinities and in a non-discriminatory fashion based on complementary electrostatic interactions.
source: By contrast, disordered polybasic PIP-binding motifs target negatively charged membranes with much weaker affinities and in a non-discriminatory fashion based on complementary electrostatic interactions (McLaughlin and Murray, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McLaughlin and Murray, 2005.

claim: αSyn-PIP binding may define a third class of interactions that is comparable in strength to folded protein domains, but driven, to large parts, by electrostatic contacts similar to those of polybasic motifs.
source: αSyn-PIP binding may define a third class of interactions that is comparable in strength to folded protein domains, but driven, to large parts, by electrostatic contacts similar to those of polybasic motifs (Galvagnion, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on comparison of binding characteristics, supported by citation.

claim: αSyn may successfully compete for cellular PIP2-PIP3 binding sites with other proteins, particularly when their abundance is in a comparable range.
source: Based on these affinity considerations, we speculate that αSyn may successfully compete for cellular PIP2-PIP3 binding sites with other proteins, particularly when their abundance is in a comparable range.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on affinity considerations.

claim: Intracellular αSyn concentrations directly influenced cellular PIP2 levels.
source: Our findings are additionally supported by recent data showing that intracellular αSyn concentrations directly influenced cellular PIP2 levels and that protein reduction diminished PIP2 abundance, whereas αSyn overexpression increased PIP2 synthesis and produced significantly elongated axons in primary cortical neurons (Schechter et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schechter et al., 2020a.

claim: αSyn protein reduction diminished PIP2 abundance.
source: Our findings are additionally supported by recent data showing that intracellular αSyn concentrations directly influenced cellular PIP2 levels and that protein reduction diminished PIP2 abundance, whereas αSyn overexpression increased PIP2 synthesis and produced significantly elongated axons in primary cortical neurons (Schechter et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schechter et al., 2020a.

claim: αSyn overexpression increased PIP2 synthesis and produced significantly elongated axons in primary cortical neurons.
source: Our findings are additionally supported by recent data showing that intracellular αSyn concentrations directly influenced cellular PIP2 levels and that protein reduction diminished PIP2 abundance, whereas αSyn overexpression increased PIP2 synthesis and produced significantly elongated axons in primary cortical neurons (Schechter et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schechter et al., 2020a.

claim: Effects of αSyn on PIP2 levels and axon elongation depended on αSyn's ability to interact with membranes and were absent in a membrane-binding-deficient mutant (K10E-K12E).
source: Conspicuously, these effects depended on αSyn's ability to interact with membranes and were absent in a membrane-binding-deficient mutant (i.e., K10E-K12E) (Schechter et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schechter et al., 2020a.

claim: PM expansions require dedicated cycles of endocytosis and exocytosis.
source: Because PM expansions require dedicated cycles of endocytosis and exocytosis (Pfenninger, 2009), αSyn-PIP interactions may contribute to both types of processes, as has been suggested earlier (Lautenschläger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pfenninger, 2009.

claim: αSyn-PIP interactions may contribute to endocytosis and exocytosis processes.
source: Because PM expansions require dedicated cycles of endocytosis and exocytosis (Pfenninger, 2009), αSyn-PIP interactions may contribute to both types of processes, as has been suggested earlier (Lautenschläger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: PM-specific αSyn-lipid interactions were confirmed by 'unroofing' experiments in SK-MEL-28 cells, where endogenous protein pools colocalized with members of the exocytosis machinery including Rab3A and synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2.
source: PM-specific αSyn-lipid interactions were additionally confirmed by 'unroofing' experiments in related SK-MEL-28 cells (Kaur and Lee, 2020), where endogenous protein pools colocalized with members of the exocytosis machinery including the known αSyn binding partners Rab3A (Chen et al., 2013) and synaptobrevin-2/VAMP2 (Burré et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaur and Lee, 2020; Chen et al., 2013; and Burré et al., 2010.

claim: Two studies implicated αSyn and αSyn-PIP2 interactions in clathrin assembly and clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Two other studies implicated αSyn and αSyn-PIP2 interactions in clathrin assembly and clathrin-mediated endocytosis, respectively (Vargas et al., 2020; Schechter et al., 2020b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vargas et al., 2020 and Schechter et al., 2020b.

claim: The findings strengthen the notion that phosphatidylinositol polyphosphates contribute to αSyn functions at the PM.
source: which further strengthens the notion that phosphatidylinositol polyphosphates contribute to αSyn functions at the PM.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined evidence from multiple studies.
